definition: The family name for techniques that make software do tasks that look like they need judgement — from hand-written rule engines to large language models. Ask which ring: rules, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI.
Behaviour learned from data instead of written by hand: the model's parameters are chosen to fit examples. Regression, trees, boosting, clustering, neural networks.
Machine learning with neural networks of many layers. Won on unstructured data (text, images, audio) because it learns its own features and scales with data and GPUs.
Deep-learning models that produce content — text, code, images, audio. Large language models are the text/code case.
A very large neural network trained to predict the next token of text. Run in a loop it generates; everything it does — and every failure — follows from that.
A function with numbers (parameters) in it, chosen by training so its outputs match known examples. Bigger models have more numbers; the idea is the same.
One of the numbers inside a model that training adjusts. A line has two; an LLM has billions. The trained set of them is the artefact you deploy.
The loop that chooses a model's parameters: run examples through, measure the loss, nudge the parameters against the gradient, repeat. Expensive and done once (or occasionally).
Using a trained model: parameters frozen, one input in, one output out. Every API call is inference; nothing learns from your requests.
One number saying how wrong the model's current parameters are on the known examples. Training exists to make it small; the formula encodes what 'wrong' means.
The training step: the gradient says how the loss changes if each parameter nudges up; move against it and the loss falls. Back-propagation computes it across all the layers of a network.
How big each training nudge is. Too small crawls, too big overshoots and diverges. A hyperparameter — chosen by measuring, not learned.
A setting chosen by the engineer rather than learned: learning rate, model size, number of trees, temperature. Set by trying, measuring and keeping what works.
Learning from examples that come with the correct answer (labels). Most classic ML in production. The labels are usually the cost and the constraint.
Learning structure from inputs alone — clustering, anomaly detection, embeddings. Cheap to start; judged by usefulness, not by a metric against labels.

An agent acts, receives a reward, and improves its policy. Powerful and data-hungry; the policy optimises the reward you wrote, not the intent you had. Used in preference tuning of chat models (RLHF).
Supervised learning where the label comes free from the data itself — for LLM pretraining, the label is the next token of the text. Why pretraining can use trillions of tokens nobody labelled.
The correct answer attached to a training example (spam / not spam, the price, breached / not). Quality and representativeness of labels bound the model.

A learned fragment of text — the unit a language model reads and writes, and the unit of cost and context. Common English words are usually one token; rare words, other languages, code and numbers split into more.
The lookup that maps text to token ids and back, before and after the model. Trained once with BPE; different models use different tokenisers, so counts are not comparable across vendors.
The algorithm that learns a tokeniser: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in the corpus. The ordered list of merges is the trained tokeniser.
What a language model computes: a probability for every possible next token given the text so far. Generation is that function run in a loop — predict, pick, append, repeat.

A fluent, plausible output with no grounds — the most likely continuation produced whether or not the model has reason for it. Not a bug to instruct away; design around it with context, verification and a refusal path.
A vector that stands for a piece of text, built so similar meanings point in similar directions. Compare with cosine similarity; the primitive under semantic search, RAG, clustering and dedup.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated. Ranks; never proves. Thresholds are model-specific and must be measured on your data.
Score a query vector against stored vectors and take the top k. Linear scan at small scale; approximate indexes (HNSW, IVF) at millions of vectors. Same model must embed both sides.

The mechanism by which each token looks at earlier tokens, weights which matter, and blends in what it took — computed fresh for every input in every layer. Why context works and why the same word can mean different things.
The neural-network architecture behind LLMs: blocks of self-attention plus a feed-forward layer, stacked. Attention is quadratic in input length; there is no state between calls.
The maximum tokens a model can look at in one call — input and output together. One fixed budget shared by the system prompt, history, retrieved content and the answer.

Dropping part of a prompt or answer to fit the context window or max_tokens. Silent when you did not choose it; make it a policy — measure, reserve room for the answer, drop deliberately, log what was dropped.
The tendency of models to attend less reliably to the middle of a very long prompt than to its start and end. Put instructions first, the question last, and retrieve rather than stuff.
Stage one of LLM training: next-token prediction over trillions of tokens of web, books and code. Where almost all capability comes from; sets the knowledge cutoff.

Continuing training on (prompt, ideal answer) examples. Gives a base model its chat shape; on your own data it changes behaviour and format more reliably than it adds facts. LoRA/PEFT train small adapters instead of all weights.
Stage three: humans (or a judge model) rank candidate answers and the model is tuned toward the preferred kind. Source of helpfulness, hedging, refusals — and sycophancy and eagerness to answer.
The date the training data stopped. Anything after it, or private, is not in the weights and can only come from the prompt.
A tuned model's tendency to agree with the premise of a question and to please. In pipelines, state facts as context and ask neutral questions.
Turning the model's next-token distribution into one token by drawing at random. Temperature, top-k and top-p are sampler settings — they change variety, not knowledge.
Divides the model's scores before they become probabilities: below 1 sharpens (favourite more likely), above 1 flattens (rare tokens get a chance), 0 is greedy. Low for tasks with a right answer.
Keep the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p, then sample from those. Adapts to how spread out the step is; top-k keeps a fixed number instead. Change one knob at a time.
Always take the most likely token (temperature 0). Repeatable at the sampler, prone to loops, and still not deterministic in production because the numbers upstream shift.
Whether a score means what it says — when the model says 0.8, is it right 80% of the time? Weak for LLM tone (confidence does not track correctness); measurable for classifiers.

Instructions hidden in data the model reads (an email, a web page, a document) that the model follows because it cannot tell your prompt from that data. Any read-and-act system has this surface; defend with trust boundaries and least-privilege tools.
Answering from material supplied in the prompt (retrieved documents, tool results) rather than from the model's memory — and being checkable against it, e.g. with citations.

Retrieve relevant passages (usually by embeddings, often hybrid with keyword search), put them in the prompt, and ask the model to answer from them with citations. Moves facts from the model's memory into the context.
Vector search combined with keyword (BM25) search and metadata filters, so exact terms and constraints are not lost to the 'gist' that embeddings capture.
Reusing the attention keys/values computed for an unchanged prompt prefix so it is not recomputed — cheaper and faster for stable system prompts and long shared context.

A model that maps features to a score for a category. Logistic regression is a weighted sum squashed into (0,1); trees ask questions; boosting stacks many small trees. A score becomes a decision only at a threshold.
Predicting a number (a price, a delay, next month's spend). Same model families as classification; error measured by size (MAE, RMSE) rather than precision/recall.
A weighted sum of features squashed into a probability. The first classifier to try: fast, explainable (the weights are the reason), often enough.
A model that asks a question about one feature, then another, and so on; a stump asks one. Readable and boundary-flexible; alone it overfits.
Many small trees fitted in sequence, each correcting the residual errors of the previous. The strongest default on tabular data.
A numeric input to a model, prepared from raw data: scaled, encoded, transformed. The feature code must be shared between training and serving, and any statistics fitted on training data only.

Putting features on comparable ranges before models that use weights or distances. Fit the scaler on training data; apply the same statistics everywhere else. Scaling decides what 'close' means for k-means and kNN.
The score at which a classifier's output becomes a decision. Nothing in the model picks it — the cost of a false alarm versus a miss does. Moving it trades precision for recall.
Rows the model never trained on, used for every evaluation number. Split first; split by time when there is time; training-set numbers flatter every model.
The four counts at one threshold: true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives. Every classification metric is arithmetic on them.
Of what the model flagged, how much was real: TP / (TP + FP). Low precision means false alarms.
Of the real cases, how many the model caught: TP / (TP + FN). Low recall means misses.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall — one number when you must have one; it hides which side is weak.
Right answers over all rows. Misleading whenever classes are imbalanced: with rare positives, 'always no' scores high and catches nothing.
Area under the ROC curve: the probability a random positive outranks a random negative. Threshold-free, so it compares models' ranking quality; use precision–recall AUC when positives are rare.

Information from the test rows (or from the future) reaching training or feature building, inflating every number. Testing on training rows, fitting scalers on all data, random splits of time-ordered data, features that encode the label.
Fitting the training rows so closely that the model fails on new ones — the gap between training and held-out performance. Deep trees and small data are the classic case.
Grouping rows by similarity without labels. Judged by whether people can name and act on the groups, not by a metric.
Clustering by repeating: assign each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its points. k is your choice; the result depends on scaling and the start.
Finding rows that do not belong. A z-score (standard deviations from the mean) is the crude, explainable first detector; isolation forests and learned baselines when 'normal' is complex.
How many standard deviations a value is from the mean. |z| > 3 is the classic 'not normal' line; assumes a roughly bell-shaped baseline.

The trained model as plain data — features, statistics, weights, threshold — with a version, stored with its evaluation metrics. Serving loads it; every prediction is logged with its version; rollback serves the previous one.
The notebook prepares features one way and the service another; predictions are silently wrong. One shared feature function, called from both places, is the fix.

The incoming data no longer looks like the training data (input drift), or the relationship itself changed. A leading indicator that you can no longer assume the model is right; outcomes are the truth. Retrain in a loop.

Layers of weighted sums and simple non-linear squashes, trained by gradient descent across all weights (back-propagation). Learns its own features; the model family behind embeddings, transformers and LLMs.
A model whose weights you can download and run yourself. Not necessarily open training data or a permissive licence — read it. Self-hosting means owning serving and hardware too.
The largest, most capable closed models, available through vendor APIs (and resold via cloud platforms). Strongest on judgement-heavy work; metered per token; versions change under you.

Running an open-weight model on GPUs you rent, behind your own inference server. Buys control over data, version and unit cost at high volume; costs capacity planning, serving infrastructure and on-call.
A service in front of every model call: auth, rate limits, quotas, routing between models, fallbacks, key hygiene, logging. Keeps the choice of vendor reversible.
A curated set of real cases with known-good outcomes, used to evaluate a model or prompt on every change. The LLM-feature equivalent of a held-out set.
Measuring a model or LLM feature on a held-out or golden set: rates, not single runs; slices, not one number; a sample you read. Without it you cannot tell a fix from a regression.
A recorded model response keyed by the request, replayed instead of calling the API. How this course shows real model output without CI needing a key; the site labels the model and date.
